letters.desc: Buckeye notes that generator-interconnection crediting was designed only as a financing mechanism, not to protect other customers from stranded cost risks. Any crediting mechanism for large loads must be structured differently to ensure credits paid back to data centers do not shift costs onto other wholesale customers.
quotes: An appropriate crediting mechanism for this purpose will need to be different from the crediting mechanism used for large generator interconnections.

letters.desc: TAPS proposes that large loads pay upgrade costs upfront but receive credits over time if their transmission usage justifies those costs. This satisfies the "higher of" principle in existing Commission policy while guarding against stranded cost risk if the large load fails to sustain its projected demand.
quotes: Under that mechanism, the large load would pay the upfront cost of any network upgrades, but it would have the opportunity to be credited back that full amount, so long as its transmission usage over time is sufficient to cover the costs.

This ensures that the large load pays the higher of either incremental costs or rolled-in transmission rates, mitigating the stranded cost risks to other wholesale customers if the large load fails to maintain a level of demand sufficient to justify the cost of the network upgrades caused by the large load.

letters.org: California Department of Water Resources State Water Project
letters.desc: DWR argues that generator-style guaranteed crediting is inappropriate for large load interconnections because credits must be tied to actual load levels over time. Any crediting design should deter over-reservation of transmission capacity.
quotes: This assignment of costs should be paired with an appropriate crediting mechanism. This crediting mechanism might vary from region-to-region, but it must be designed to keep wholesale customers whole and disincentivize speculative load that will impose costs on wholesale customers.
Such a guaranteed crediting mechanism should not be adopted for large load interconnections because these credits are not tied to particular levels of usage.

letters.desc: JCA oppose using the TAPS/Harvard ELI crediting mechanism for Supplemental Projects, arguing it would not guarantee that large load developers pay the full cost of network upgrades as required by the Ratepayer Protection Pledge.
quotes: If FERC decides to change its rate policy, it should not adopt the credit mechanism advanced by TAPS and Harvard ELI over the Expansion Rate Policy for incremental network upgrades built as part of Supplemental Projects.

letters.desc: TAPS warns that copying the generator interconnection crediting mechanism would fail to protect other customers from stranded costs because that mechanism was designed as a financing tool, not a cost-causation safeguard. Any credit offset must be tailored to the risk that a data center does not sustain expected demand.
quotes: the Commission cannot achieve this goal by merely copying the existing crediting mechanisms used for different purposes in the different context of generator interconnections.
any crediting mechanism must account for the unique risks and characteristics of large data center loads to protect other customers.

letters.desc: WIRES observes that a mechanism reimbursing large loads for network upgrade costs would effectively restore NITS obligations and thus eliminate the cost shift, but would also negate the policy goal of direct assignment.
quotes: establishing a crediting mechanism for large load customers would effectively reimburse them for any network upgrade costs that they were responsible for. Once they have been fully reimbursed, they would presumably then be responsible for NITS obligations like any other customers.
